## [§5.3.b] Trial with penalty — definition and logic

I call it a trial. with penalty. That sounds ugly. That's how I' call it internally. You wouldn't say that to somebody. But it's a trial with penalty. So basically, a customer can try out your product or service for free so long as they meet your terms. For comparison, the win-your-money-back offer, the attraction offer, gives customers the chance to get their money back if they meet the terms. In a trial with penalty offer, customers only pay if they don't meet the terms. So the win-your-money-back and the free trial with penalty are virtually the same offer; we're just changing when they pay and how they pay. So they'll mirror the actions and results that you used in win-your-money-back, but this time, we use avoiding fees rather than winning your money back as the incentive for adherence. So they avoid penalties rather than get or losing their money that they paid originally. All right, so with a trial with penalty, this isn't, "Here's my thing, see if you like it." ## [§3.3.a] How I learned it — the scholarship / partial-scholarship story

So our next attraction offer is free giveaways. So I'm gonna go over how I learned it, description, examples, important points, and summary. So let's dive in. So how I learned this. So I, uh, I was talking to, um, a business owner, and he was telling me about this, you know, crazy play that he had that was working really, really well. And I was like, "Okay, well, how does it, work?" And he said, "So basically, I give away a scholarship for my year-long flagship thing, um, if people kind of opt in. And they have to, you know, answer a couple questions about their business, why I should pick them, et' cetera." He said, "So then I do, you know, a countdown, and then I do a drawing, um, and I do a live webinar where I re-, you know, release it live, sell people on how great it is." And so after he, he, he told me, he's like, "Okay, so I picked the person," and I was like, "Yeah, but okay, so you just give something away for free. Like, how does that, how does that actually, you know, uh, make you any money in. the business?" And he said, "Well, the key is. the, uh, participation trophy," or said differently, "The partial scholarship." And so he's like, "So what I, do is, I reach out to all the people who opted in, uh, and filled out all these questions about why they should be eligible, their pain points, their aspirations, their dreams, why they should be qualified, why this is important to them." He's like, "And then I just do a second countdown for people who have partial scholarships, uh, for them to basically, redeem those. And that partial scholarship is a discount off of the, uh, value that I advertise and, uh, for my grand prize, right? Of the full scholarship." And so that structure, I was like, "Oh," and he said, "And here's the great part. I use the same structure that I give to, the online fitness trainers so that they do, the same thing when they get customers." So they just say, "Hey, I'm doing a, a one-year transformation," or whatever it is, and then they have a bunch of people opt in for it, and they do partial scholarships for everybody else. And so this clearly became this repeatable framework of grand prize, participation trophy, or grand prize, promotional offer. So you promote the main thing, and then you give some sort of discount off the main thing for people who ask for or are qualified for that main offer. And so this gives you an amazing way to generate tons of leads. It gives you a very cool way to ethically sell how amazing something is." Like, if I s-, if I get up on, stage and say, "Hey, I've got this amazing thing," I talk of how great it is, that's one thing. Now, if everybody in the audience knows that, they're waiting for me to pick one of them to win this thing, they are way more engaged, they're way more leaning in, because they're imagining them actually, winning it. So you have kind of a different level of receptivity, which is what I think makes this so powerful. And you also get a ton of goodwill, 'cause you're like, giving stuff away, right? So it's just, it's an awesome, awesome play. Now to be clear though, this is, this is something that is so powerful that it is, uh, legally, um, regulated, all right? Because if you do one of these and you charge for it, it's called an illegal lottery, all right? And so like, these things work well enough that the laws had to get made to, uh, to show, uh, how not to do them the wrong way.
